In the run-up to November's congressional elections, Trump is aiming to show that his policies have bolstered jobs and manufacturing. [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"Polls have shown"] that Trump's Republicans have lost voter support, largely over cost-of-living concerns. The president has said his tariffs and industrial policy will revive US factory work, from steelmaking to shipbuilding. Anduril's location in Maryland was formerly home to a large steel mill that went through decades of financial decline and closed in bankruptcy in 2012. Trump is touring the country in a pre-election blitz, announcing or claiming credit for a range of private-sector investments and government spending initiatives he has called "goodies." END-OF-DECADE TARGET The new plant, dubbed Arsenal-2, is expected to be operational by the end of the decade. Anduril is building another facility in California to manufacture Virginia-class submarine components, and plans to expand into producing larger submarine modules and hull sections once its Baltimore shipyard becomes operational. Virginia-class submarines, which can travel at speeds exceeding 25 knots, are the Navy's latest generation of nuclear-powered attack submarines, designed for anti-submarine warfare, land-attack strikes and surveillance missions. General Dynamics' (GD.N) Electric Boat and Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII.N) jointly build them. Anduril, founded in 2017 by Palmer Luckey, is best known for its autonomous systems, drones and software built for the US military and its allies. Anduril's $1 billion [USN:L1N4070RY TEXT:"Arsenal-1 facility"] in Ohio began producing autonomous combat drones this year.

item.title: For Trump’s Treasury, the sting is in the auction ‘tail’: McGeever
item.description: US Treasury auctions are supposed to be dull, predictable, and non-newsworthy affairs. But these are not normal times, and the Trump administration now risks seeing weak debt sales make headline news.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: US Treasury auctions are supposed to be dull, predictable, and non-newsworthy affairs. But these are not normal times, and the Trump administration now risks seeing weak debt sales make headline news. The Treasury plans to sell nearly $120 billion of debt this week, the first sales outside of T-bills in two weeks: $58 billion of three-year notes on Tuesday, $39 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday, and $22 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday. These might normally be non-events, but they're under increasing scrutiny because the September 22-24 auctions were remarkably weak, particularly the five-year note auction on Sept. 23, which helped spark the biggest rise in bond yields since April last year. Yields have not come down since and have instead powered ahead to multi-decade highs across most maturities. It's worth stating that there's next to zero chance that the US would ever have a "failed" debt auction. Primary dealers – the 26 Wall Street banks and institutions currently approved by the New York Fed as Treasury market makers – will always participate. They effectively underwrite the sales, ensuring the $30 trillion US debt market – the most liquid market in the world – functions smoothly. This, in turn, keeps the entire global financial system chugging along, as well. Trillions of dollars of global debt, assets, and market derivatives use Treasuries as a reference. US government bonds are also the collateral used to lubricate the pipes of US and global financial plumbing - repo agreements, interbank lending, and funding. In short, as long as US debt is the lynchpin of the global financial system, there will always be buyers at Treasury auctions. The issue, as ever, is the price at which these sales clear. Right now, borrowing costs on the secondary market are the highest since the mid to early 2000s, so it is reasonable to assume that Treasury will pay comparably high rates on the primary market. But as the most recent auctions have shown, there is also still room for negative surprises. TOO BIG TO TAIL? The $70 billion sale of five-year notes on September 23 was one of the most alarming in recent memory. Demand as measured by the 'bid-to-cover' ratio was the lowest in nine years. Treasury ultimately sold the notes at 5.033%, which was more than three basis points above the market yield at the bidding deadline. Three basis points might not sound like a lot, but for a five-year auction, that’s extraordinary. It was the largest so-called "tail" since June 2022. To find the last time a five-year auction had a 3 bps "tail," JP Morgan analysts note, you have to go all the way back to 2011, when a brewing debt ceiling crisis would lead to a credit rating downgrade that August. Moving back to the present, concerns about the dire US fiscal outlook have pushed up long-term borrowing costs. As a result, the Trump administration is widely expected to gradually shift the weight of the Treasury’s huge borrowing requirements towards the shorter - and cheaper - end of the curve. This is why the five-year auction two weeks ago caused such alarm. "Tails" of 3 bps are common in longer bond auctions, but not in sales of debt that sit right in the so-called "belly" of the yield curve. If Treasury is being forced to pay higher premiums to shift these notes, then Houston, we have a problem. Fat auction “tails” can be a result of multiple forces, including market volatility on the day itself or more worrying fundamental issues that might erode demand over time. It's often difficult to untangle the two dynamics, as they are not mutually exclusive. On a more optimistic note, these jitters haven’t migrated to the front end of the curve. Yet. Three-year and 10-year yields are up around 50 basis points from their last auctions a month ago, hovering around 4.96% and 5.32%, respectively. The 30-year yield is up around 35 bps at 5.65%. That should be high enough to attract solid demand and ensure smooth sales, right? Probably. But if there’s a sting in the tails, volatility and uncertainty could bite across the market. Investors will be watching like, well, hawks. (The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters) Enjoying this column? item.title: Sweden to deploy Patriot missiles to NATO hub in Poland
item.description: Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said on Tuesday the Nordic country will deploy Patriot missile defence systems to eastern Poland to help protect the NATO logistics hub that supplies weapons to Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said on Tuesday the Nordic country will deploy Patriot missile defence systems to eastern Poland to help protect the NATO logistics hub that supplies weapons to Ukraine. Sweden will replace Patriot support from the Netherlands and the operation will start in December. It will deploy around 100 military personnel from the air defence unit in Halmstad, the government said Sweden [USN:L6N45M0TU TEXT:"last week announced"] that it was deploying Gripen fighter jets to Poland as part of a NATO airspace surveillance mission "The task of both the Gripen deployment and the Patriot deployment is...to protect NATO's logistics hub in Poland at the airport," Kristersson said Sweden declined to say how many Patriot system units would be sent to Poland Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk [USN:L8N4590UT TEXT:"said last month"], citing unnamed intelligence agencies, that Russia plans to launch 'hybrid' drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine Russia's President Vladimir Putin said last week that Russia had "no intention of attacking anyone...but if we are subjected to aggression, we will have no choice but to respond" (This story has been refiled to replace an incorrect image.)

item.title: Paramount wraps up mega Warner Bros merger to create Hollywood powerhouse Skydance
item.description: Paramount Skydance on Tuesday completed its blockbuster $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros Discovery , creating a Hollywood heavyweight that hands CEO David Ellison control of one of the world's largest entertainment and news businesses.
item.dc:creator: Anzar Mehraj, Harshita Varghese
item.content:encoded: Paramount Skydance (PSKY.O) on Tuesday completed its blockbuster $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros Discovery (WBD.O) , creating a Hollywood heavyweight that hands CEO David Ellison control of one of the world's largest entertainment and news businesses. The deal brings together the studios behind "Mission: Impossible," "Harry Potter" and DC Studios alongside major television and streaming networks such as CBS, CNN, Paramount+ and HBO Max — forming an expansive entertainment company spanning film, TV and news. Ellison laid out his vision for the new company in a memo to employees on Tuesday in which he said the acquisition is "to build the next-generation media and entertainment company, powered by creativity and technology." The goal, he added, was not simply to get bigger but "to take on the biggest players in our industry." The new company, called Skydance, is the latest iteration of a conglomerate once controlled by the late Sumner Redstone that has precipitously shrunk over the years, as audiences flock to news and entertainment delivered by a growing cadre of smaller publishers and creators chipping away at once-mighty Hollywood. Skydance not only faces competition from Netflix, Disney and others, but also from tech giants Apple, Meta, and Amazon, as well as the growing threat of AI. Shares of the combined company moved to the New York Stock Exchange from Nasdaq on Tuesday to trade under the ticker "SKYD." [USN:L4N45D11C TEXT:"Settlements"] with a [USN:L4N45D112 TEXT:"coalition of US states"] and a Hollywood writers union removed the main legal barriers to the merger, one of the largest in media history. It comes as Hollywood faces declining cable-TV subscriptions, the high cost of competing for streaming audiences and persistent pressure from unions over jobs and creative workers' rights. TRUMP'S CNN PROBLEM President Donald Trump expressed approval when asked about the deal. "It's going to be a great company," he told reporters . "That's a great merger. I'm glad they let it go." Trump has attacked news organizations since his first term and recently took the unprecedented step of [USN:L8N45A1OV TEXT:"banning several news outlets"] from the White House, including CNN. The move came weeks ahead of the November 3 midterm elections in which Trump's fellow Republicans are defending narrow majorities in Congress. CNN chief Mark Thompson and CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss [USN:L4N45R0RX TEXT:"will continue"] in their respective leadership roles in the new company and each will separately report to Ellison and Kreiz, allaying [USN:L1N42I0HA TEXT:"concerns from critics"] that Weiss, who took over as CBS News editor-in-chief in 2025, would have greater control over all of Skydance's news operations. The concerns are also fueled by [USN:L1N43G107 TEXT:"lawmakers' criticism of Ellison"] for tailoring news coverage at Paramount-owned CBS News to favor Trump. As part of the settlement, Ellison agreed to create an editorial independence board to oversee CNN and CBS. Experts warn that the board will be "[USN:L4N45E0EO TEXT:"toothless"]." Ellison [USN:L6N45R0UG TEXT:"said last week"] the Skydance name was chosen to retain the individual identities of Paramount and Warner Bros studios, rather than combining them under a new brand. Wall Street analysts, however, said the name reinforces the extent of Ellison's control, highlighting how some of Hollywood's most iconic brands now answer to him and how he has a platform to impose his strategy and culture. In just 16 years, Skydance has gone from an independent studio to the center of one of Hollywood's biggest power plays. Founded in 2010 by the son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, it built its reputation as a financial backer and producer of Paramount's blockbuster "Top Gun: Maverick." After [USN:L4N3TZ1NM TEXT:"merging with"] Paramount last year, Skydance set its sights on Warner Bros, entering a heated bidding contest with Netflix (NFLX.O) while drawing interest from other potential suitors, including Comcast (CMCSA.O) . Warner Bros shareholders received an additional $41.9 million in a "ticking fee," based on the number of days between September-end and the deal-closing, according to a regulatory filing. BROADER HOLLYWOOD BET Ellison named Mattel's former CEO Ynon Kreiz as Skydance co-CEO to run day-to-day operations and lead the integration, while Ellison oversees creative direction and overall strategy. Kreiz was also appointed to the company's board on Tuesday, alongside former Activision Blizzard CEO Bobby Kotick. Former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair will join the company as an adviser, it said. In bringing on Kreiz, Ellison has signaled the [USN:L4N45N0LV TEXT:"need for a cost-cutter"]. The duo faces the task of combining two large companies while delivering $6 billion in planned savings, a big part of which Paramount said would come from "non-labor sources." That includes combining technology and cloud providers of the two companies, but the scale of the cuts is expected to affect jobs across Hollywood. Skydance plans to combine its streaming services, including HBO Max and Paramount+, into a single service and has [USN:L1N45D0VR TEXT:"pledged to release at least 30 films"] each in the first two years after closing, rising to 32 a year for the following three. The combined company is also expected to carry about $80 billion in debt, putting pressure on Ellison to grow streaming, preserve cash flow from cable networks and improve theatrical film performance. Analysts at MoffettNathanson forecast profit, or EBITDA, of $16 billion for 2028 and rising to $19 billion in 2030. The research firm also predicted about $67 billion in revenue in 2028, growing to roughly $70 billion in 2030. Ellison's annual base salary will be $5 million, with a target annual bonus of $5 million, according to the filing.

item.title: Euroleague shareholders reject NBA Europe offer, door open for future talks
item.description: Europe’s biggest basketball clubs snubbed an offer to team up with the NBA on Tuesday, raising the prospect of a battle for the continent’s top teams, players and commercial riches.
item.dc:creator: Elvira Pollina
item.content:encoded: Europe’s biggest basketball clubs snubbed an offer to team up with the NBA on Tuesday, raising the prospect of a battle for the continent’s top teams, players and commercial riches. Sources familiar with the discussions told Reuters that the Euroleague's shareholder clubs rejected a collaboration offer from the NBA, though the door on a deal was not yet closed. Representatives of the 13 permanent shareholder clubs met near Lake Como, with the NBA proposal dominating discussions about the future of European basketball. In separate decisions at the meeting, the clubs agreed to convert into franchises but stopped short of formally approving an expansion of the competition from 20 to 24 teams, the Euroleague said in a statement. The move to a franchise model will give the clubs a more permanent stake in the competition than their existing long-term licences. A person attending the meeting told Reuters the decision on allocating additional long-term licences would be taken within the next month. Up to eight could be awarded and the remaining places would be filled through a combination of short-term licences, wildcards and sporting qualification through the BKT EuroCup. The Euroleague is eager to press ahead with expansion, the source said, turning attention to whether the NBA will submit a revised proposal before those decisions are made. A senior sports executive told Reuters any collaboration was unlikely to begin before 2028 because it would be difficult to organise a new competition in time for the 2027-28 season. The Euroleague did not refer to the widely reported NBA offer in its statement but told Reuters last Friday it remained open to collaboration. Although the clubs rejected the current proposal, talks with the NBA could continue. Reuters was not immediately able to confirm the details of the NBA's offer, but media reports said it envisaged the NBA's continental expansion project merging with the Euroleague. The NBA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. NBA Europe's managing director, George Aivazoglou, is due to speak at a conference in London on Thursday. FIBA, basketball's global governing body, said it would not comment at this stage. The rejection is a significant setback to efforts to combine Europe's established elite basketball competition with the financial and commercial power of the NBA, which plans to launch a 16-team NBA Europe league in 2027. SURGE OF INTEREST The NBA has stepped up its push into Europe amid a surge of interest in the sport, with Euroleague reporting in May an 82% increase in TV viewership through the first 25 regular-season rounds of the 2025-26 campaign. The NBA has also enjoyed growing momentum on the continent. Streaming deals with providers like Amazon Prime have boosted audiences for the NBA in Europe, while regular-season games in Berlin and London this year highlighted the league's growing appeal. Viewership of January's clash between Orlando Magic and Memphis Grizzlies in London was up 90% compared to the last NBA game there in 2019. A report from JB Capital commissioned by the Euroleague values the competition at €1.41 billion ($1.59 billion), while the aggregate value of its licensed teams was put at approximately €1.8 billion. Those figures pale in comparison to the NBA. The NBA recently surpassed Major League Baseball to become the world's second-richest sports league, according to Sports Value, a marketing and valuation agency, with upwards of $14 billion in revenue during the 2025-26 season. The NBA and Euroleague have said throughout this year they want to collaborate on a new competition, but both have also made clear they are prepared to pursue their own plans if no agreement is reached. They have set no formal deadline, although both sides have indicated they want greater clarity by the end of the season. The expansion drive extends the NBA's [USN:L1N3QQ016 TEXT:"longstanding effort"] towards globalisation, a trend that has emerged across North America's "Big Four" men's professional leagues, with the NFL launching a [USN:L6N44U08L TEXT:"record slate"] of nine international games this season. ($1 = 0.8883 euros)

item.title: Rubio tells Russia to share more information about plague death
item.description: Russia should share more information about the death of a plague laboratory worker who died last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday, in an incident Washington was watching "very closely".
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia should share more information about the death of a [USN:S8N45F09U TEXT:"plague laboratory worker"] who died last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday, in an incident Washington was watching "very closely". A laboratory worker at Siberia's plague research institute fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on Friday, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people and sparking public health fears on social media. Russian authorities have said the situation is under control. "I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," Rubio told reporters in Iceland. "We're watching it very closely, hour by hour." Rubio said the US has measures available to help Russia if the situation turns out to be more serious than has so far been acknowledged, but needed to know more before it could step in. President Donald Trump told reporters on Tuesday he had a call scheduled very soon with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin. When asked what intelligence agencies were saying about the situation in Russia, Trump replied: "So far we are in very deep discussions, we'll be able to report about it probably tomorrow."

item.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq reach record closing highs as focus pivots to earnings
item.description: US stocks ended higher on Tuesday as crude prices steadied and US Treasury yields eased, offering some reprieve from concerns that have preoccupied investors in recent weeks, and allowing markets to turn their attention to the approaching third-quarter reporting season.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Culp, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
item.content:encoded: US stocks ended higher on Tuesday as crude prices steadied and US Treasury yields eased, offering some reprieve from concerns that have preoccupied investors in recent weeks, and allowing markets to turn their attention to the approaching third-quarter reporting season. The broad rally pushed the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq to all-time closing highs. The blue-chip Dow remains just over 5% shy of its record closing level reached on August 5. When oil prices stabilize or move lower, "that causes yields to move down because there's less anxiety about energy-driven inflation, which in turn is helping lift stocks higher," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice president at Wealthspire Advisors in New York. "This has been the narrative of the market for the last couple of weeks." Six of the "Magnificent Seven" group of AI-linked megacap firms advanced, bolstering gains, while small-caps (.RUT) lagged their larger-cap counterparts. The AI trade is very much alive, with the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index (.SOX) gaining ground. Expenditures on AI-related infrastructure were reflected in international trade data, which showed imports of capital goods rose by 4.4% in August. The Commerce Department's report showed the [USN:L1N45S0IV TEXT:"US trade deficit"] grew by 13.7% as imports rose to a record high. On monthly and annual bases, imports have grown by 4.3% and 28.4%, respectively, reflecting robust domestic demand that could exacerbate inflation pressures, particularly amid war-related supply constraints. Even so, financial markets are currently pricing in a diminishing probability of 19.4% that the US Federal Reserve will implement its second consecutive rate hike at this month's monetary policy meeting, down from 50.9% a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool. Fed rate hike bets have been responsive to [USN:L1N45S05E TEXT:"oil prices"], which have surged amid the Iran war, threatening to morph into broader price pressures. But supply worries eased after the Group of Seven countries reached an agreement to release emergency diesel and crude stockpiles, helping to stabilize front-month WTI and Brent crude futures. "We don't expect (the Fed) to do anything at the next meeting," said Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder in New York. "But I think they're in a gradual hiking cycle." "High oil prices have hit a broad range of consumers," Ghriskey added. "That's one of the reasons for the recent Fed hike." The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 253.14 points, or 0.49%, to 51,521.04, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 45.00 points, or 0.58%, to 7,818.95 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 122.48 points, or 0.45%, to 27,599.79. Of the 11 major sectors in the S&P 500, all but healthcare (.SPXHC) gained ground, with utilities (.SPLCRU) leading the way. Third-quarter earnings season kicks off next week, with a number of high-profile financial firms expected to report next Tuesday. Analysts currently expect annual S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.6%, in aggregate, for the July-to-September period, led by an expected 114.7% jump in energy earnings, followed by a 66.5% estimated surge in tech results, according to LSEG. Marvell Technology (MRVL.O) climbed 5.8% following the [USN:L6N45S0Y5 TEXT:"chip designer's"] 2028 revenue forecast hike due to strong demand for its data center chips. Chipmaker AMD (AMD.O) gained 2.8% after CEO Lisa Su said [USN:L6N45S09C TEXT:"it plans"] to substantially increase its chip supply in 2027 to meet booming AI demand. Constellation Energy (CEG.O) jumped 12.3% after Alphabet (GOOGL.O) entered into a 3,590-megawatt power [USN:L6N45S04O TEXT:"deal"] with the company. Option Care Health (OPCH.O) soared 32.7% after drug distributor McKesson (MCK.N) and private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice [USN:L4N45S0SZ TEXT:"agreed to buy"] the infusion therapy provider in a deal worth about $5.8 billion, including debt. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.93-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. There were 258 new highs and 219 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,394 stocks rose and 2,378 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.01-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 23 new 52-week highs and 2 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 61 new highs and 182 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.50 billion shares, compared with the 17.51 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

item.title: Americans deeply skeptical of taxpayer-funded election ads, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
item.description: An overwhelming majority of Americans said that it is inappropriate to use taxpayer funds for TV ads featuring the president around an election, in a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted as spots with President Donald Trump air ahead of November's midterms.
item.dc:creator: Trevor Hunnicutt, Jason Lange
item.content:encoded: An overwhelming majority of Americans said that it is inappropriate to use taxpayer funds for TV ads featuring the president around an election, in a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted as spots with President Donald Trump air ahead of November's midterms. The six-day poll, which concluded on Monday, found that 86% of Americans — and four out of five Republicans — think it is inappropriate to use taxpayer money to pay for election-related TV ads featuring the president or his cabinet. Ethics experts and lawmakers from both parties have criticized three nationally broadcast ads that celebrate a "golden age of America" airing weeks before the November 3 midterm elections . Lawmakers have questioned whether public funds are being used to promote Trump politically, while other critics say the spots may violate longstanding restrictions on government propaganda and political activity. Trump and his aides have said the ads are educational, patriotic and not intended to promote any politician's candidacy. "These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad," said a White House spokesperson who declined to be named. Trump said late on Monday that he would pay for ads himself or with money raised from the MAGA political committee. A White House official said on Tuesday that Trump was referring to the MAGA Inc PAC paying for future ads but did not plan to reimburse taxpayers for the ads that the government has paid for in recent weeks. One ad features Trump declaring that "America will never be a communist country" while a chorus repeats "love me." Another combines images of Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising a "golden age of America." A third describes a "final battle" against the "deep state" and closely resembles one of Trump's 2024 campaign advertisements. Each ad ends with a disclaimer that it was paid for by the US government. Democratic lawmakers have sought independent investigations and said that the White House [USN:L1N45N046 TEXT:"transferred $20 million"] in Homeland Security Department funds to air the ads. PRESSURE ON REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF ELECTIONS Republicans seeking reelection face growing pressure as the president's approval rating sits at [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"record lows"]. Trump has taken a series of unusual steps in recent months promoting his brand and accomplishments, including a [USN:L6N41H110 TEXT:"sweeping makeover of Washington."] A Trump-appointed board [USN:L1N4560T6 TEXT:"shut down"] the capital's landmark John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts after courts rejected two plans to put the president's name on the building. Some 71% of respondents oppose renaming the Kennedy Center to include Trump's name, the poll showed. Just a quarter of Republicans supported that idea. "For me to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition," Trump said last month. A MEDIA BAN AT THE WHITE HOUSE In September, Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House before a judge ordered the administration to [USN:L1N45G0ZE TEXT:"restore their access"]. Republicans were more supportive of keeping some reporters out of the White House, with 57% backing the practice. Democrats and independents were overwhelmingly opposed. Overall, 68% of respondents said the practice was inappropriate. The Justice Department has accused the outlets of threatening national security with their coverage, citing stories about US missile stockpiles, construction of Trump's White House ballroom and turnout at the recent Republican midterm convention. The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, gathered responses from 4,506 US adults and had a margin of error of about 2 percentage points.

item.title: ASOS shares slide after hackers target online retailer
item.description: Shares in ASOS fell 10% on Tuesday after the British online fashion retailer warned that some customer information may have been accessed following the unauthorised sending of a notification to shoppers.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Shares in ASOS (ASOS.L) fell 10% on Tuesday after the British online fashion retailer warned that some customer information may have been accessed following the unauthorised sending of a notification to shoppers. The group said it was investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that it uses to communicate with customers. It said it took immediate action to restrict access to the platforms and was working with internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities. "Basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed. We do not believe that payment-card information or account passwords, were impacted," it said. The retailer's website and app were operating as normal, with no current disruption to operations, it said. British companies and institutions have been increasingly hit by aggressive and regular cyber and ransomware attacks in recent years. The British Library, a blood testing service, the London Underground, Marks & Spencer (MKS.L) , the Co-op and Jaguar Land Rover are some that have suffered months of disruption due to such breaches. HACKING GROUP 'XUANYE GROUP' CLAIMS RESPONSIBILITY The notifications to ASOS shoppers - addressed to ASOS' data protection officer and IT department - read, "we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it." Snowflake is a data storage firm, whose tools are used by thousands of companies. A hacking group calling itself the "Xuanye group" claimed credit for compromising ASOS' Snowflake repository in the push alert sent to users of the retailer's app. The message included a link to a Telegram channel, where the group said that payment information "is not affected," and that the ASOS app "is safe to use." "The incident involves customer information, it is safe on our server, and it will not be touched for a designated period," the group said in a message posted to the channel. A spokesperson for Snowflake said it launched an investigation as soon as it became aware of the notification. "At this time, we can report that we have found no compromise of the Snowflake platform." Hackers have previously targeted organisations' Snowflake data repositories. In 2024, Google's (GOOGL.O) cybersecurity unit Mandiant detailed a widespread hacking spree targeting Snowflake data associated with at least 165 customers. ASOS said that it has cyber insurance, including basic continuity insurance, but said it was too early to quantify any potential impact on trading. Shares in the group were up more than 60% so far this year, though they are well below a peak in 2018 amid tough competition in fast fashion. The company has been divesting assets and last month provided an upbeat profit forecast for fiscal 2026.

item.title: Californians blast Trump remark that Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles, San Diego
item.description: President Donald Trump suggested to a crowd of his supporters in Nebraska that Iran could "take out" a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego, drawing a swift rebuke from California's Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans.
item.dc:creator: Steve Gorman, Bo Erickson
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump suggested to a crowd of his supporters in Nebraska that Iran could "take out" a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego, drawing a swift rebuke from California's Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans. Trump, speaking at a [USN:L1N45R0ZC TEXT:"political rally"] in the state's farm belt on Monday, discussed American wartime economic sacrifices and said he was determined to "see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did." "And again, remember, with the war, it's just artificial, it's a little bit high, it's a small price to pay," he told the crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, apparently referring to rising prices of fuel, fertilizer and other products attributed to energy market disruptions from the war. "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, let 'em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it's going to be over with very soon," he said. "It's essentially almost over with," Trump went on. "But it's going to end very soon, and it's going to end one way or the other." On Tuesday, the White House dismissed criticism of the remark. "The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," White House Director of Communications Steven Cheung said in a social media post. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money." Trump has shrugged off cost-of-living concerns stemming from the Iran conflict before, and he previously downplayed his concerns about the potential for Iran or its allies to launch an attack on US soil. EARLY VOTING UNDERWAY IN CALIFORNIA The comment in rural Nebraska, a state Trump won with more than 55% of the vote in the 2024 presidential election, targeted Democratic-run cities in California, a solidly Democratic state the president often criticizes. Monday's comments prompted a backlash from California officials. California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, denounced the Republican president as "deranged and dangerous." "After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego," he wrote on X. Newsom, who has positioned himself as a major political foil to Trump and is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, juxtaposed a video clip of Trump in Nebraska with mention of the president's previous rhetoric to justify deploying US military troops to Los Angeles and other cities to fight crime and enforce immigration. California's early voting for the November midterm elections started on Monday. The president's Republican Party has hoped to win more races in the state in recent years, including this year's gubernatorial election. Newsom championed the redrawing of California's [USN:S0N3WN09U TEXT:"congressional map"] last year to favor Democrats in this year's election after Trump pushed for conservative-led Texas to [USN:L1N3TX13Y TEXT:"redraw its map"] to boost Republicans. One of the Republicans running in a competitive race in a redrawn California district near San Diego, Jim Desmond, distanced himself from Trump's remarks. "I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland," he wrote on X. "No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage." US Representative Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in a competitive race in northern California, said in a statement that Trump's comment was "unhelpful." Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, said in a statement that Trump's comment "could potentially compromise our safety." Appearing on MS Now on Tuesday, Bass disputed Cheung's assertion that Trump's comments were being misinterpreted by a "freaked out" media. "Well, I'm not sure that he understands that we can hear what the president said," Bass countered, adding that Cheung's defense of Trump's remarks "has no connection to the words that came out of the president's mouth." Los Angeles and San Diego rank as the largest and second-largest cities in California by population. More than 115,000 active-duty service members are also stationed in San Diego, including Naval Base San Diego, the largest on the US west coast. "My constituents — including many active duty service members, veterans, and their families — are not acceptable collateral damage in Trump’s stupid war," US Representative Sara Jacobs, a Democrat, said in a social media post. (This story has been refiled to fix the dateline to Oct 6, not Oct 5.)

item.title: Italy regulator probes AI music startup Suno over terms of service
item.description: Italy's antitrust authority said on Tuesday it had opened an investigation into AI music startup Suno, saying some clauses in its terms of service may be unfair to consumers.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Italy's antitrust authority said on Tuesday it had opened an investigation into AI music startup Suno, saying some clauses in its terms of service may be unfair to consumers. Suno was not immediately available for comment Suno's terms could create a significant imbalance in the rights and obligations of users, the watchdog said They give Suno "broad discretion" to unilaterally modify its contract, service and subscription prices without having to provide any justification, it added in a statement The regulator said the licence granted by users was excessively broad and included a waiver of moral rights that may conflict with Italian copyright law Suno's terms require users to resolve disputes through mandatory arbitration in the United States, waive class-action rights and accept Massachusetts as the exclusive jurisdiction for legal claims, the authority said It added it would launch a consultation in the coming weeks in which interested business groups, chambers of commerce and consumer associations could participate

item.title: UK watchdog opens first Online Safety Act probe into Meta
item.description: Britain's communications regulator opened its first formal investigation into Meta under the Online Safety Act on Tuesday, questioning whether it properly assessed risks posed by its Instagram Instants feature before launching it in May.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sandle
item.content:encoded: Britain's communications regulator opened its first formal investigation into Meta under the Online Safety Act on Tuesday, questioning whether it properly assessed risks posed by its Instagram Instants feature before launching it in May. Instants allows content shared by users on Instagram to disappear after being viewed. Ofcom said its investigation would establish whether Meta carried out a "suitable and sufficient" assessment of the risks of illegal content on the feature and any risks posed to children before its launch. George Lusty, director of enforcement at Ofcom, said: "Our online safety laws are clear — significant changes to platforms must be risk assessed before they're launched." Safety by design had to be built in and not bolted on, he said. "Today's investigation shows we'll take action where we have concerns that providers are failing to comply," he said. Meta said it took its regulatory obligations under the Online Safety Act seriously. "We conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom about this feature on a number of occasions before launching it," a spokesperson said. "Instants has in-built protections, including blocking screenshots, reshares and forwarding, no public feed, and Teen Account protections on automatically." "We will of course co-operate with Ofcom during this investigation," the spokesperson said. Ofcom's first investigation under the Online Safety Act was into an online suicide discussion forum last year, followed by probes into pornography sites, file-sharing services used to distribute child sexual abuse material, and platforms such as 4chan. Britain's online safety regime sets obligations for social media platforms, search engines and adult content providers to tackle illegal content and to protect children's safety. Ofcom requires companies to conduct risk assessments and implement safety measures, such as age verification. If a company fails to comply, Ofcom can impose fines of up to £18 million or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is greater. Meta has launched legal challenges against Ofcom over its implementation of the act, including the scale and scope of information it has to provide to the regulator and the level of fees Ofcom charges. In January, Ofcom launched an investigation into Meta over the provision of information about its WhatsApp Business product under a separate Communications Act.

item.title: School protests sweeping France cause 'heaviest toll in decades'
item.description: Demonstrations swept across France on Tuesday as teachers and parents took to the streets with high school pupils on the biggest day of what Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described as the most violent student demonstrations in decades.
item.dc:creator: Tilman Blasshofer, Cecile Mantovani, Lucien Libert
item.content:encoded: Demonstrations swept across France on Tuesday as teachers and parents took to the streets with high school pupils on the biggest day of what Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described as the most violent student demonstrations in decades. Police fired tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups on the fringes of marches in Paris, Strasbourg, Rennes and Toulouse, among other cities. The marches drew more than 250,000 people in dozens of cities, the interior ministry said, though organisers said 450,000 had participated. The protests, in which a teenager lost a hand on Monday, were the latest manifestation of public anger in a country where support for populist parties on the far right and far left has surged ahead of a presidential election in the spring. The government is under pressure to tame public debt amid weak growth, and has struggled with basic tasks such as passing a budget since President Emmanuel Macron's allies lost their majority in a 2024 parliamentary vote. Lecornu told lawmakers at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had so far been injured in clashes, "the heaviest toll in decades paid by the school system". His office said more than 700 police officers were also hurt. Macron has convened Lecornu and other senior ministers at an emergency meeting on Tuesday, broadcaster BFM reported. US President Donald Trump said the protests were evidence of "out of control" migration in France. "This isn't about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country," he posted on Truth Social. The students' demands do not concern religion or immigration, but focus instead on understaffing and lack of funding. Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party has not linked the protests to France's migration policy. Lecornu's office did not respond to a request for comment. In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up handmade signs bearing phrases such as "The state has killed national education". In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city. Paris police said clashes in the capital resulted from some 300 people, most hooded or masked, facing off against security forces, and that the protest generally unfolded without major incident elsewhere. Several storefronts were damaged. The Interior Ministry said 488 people had been arrested and 48 security personnel were injured on Tuesday. MAINTENANCE COMPLAINTS The student protests began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris before spreading nationwide. Students complain about schools facing basic maintenance problems, from water leaks to rat infestations. "There is such a gap between the elites and us," said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high-school graduate in Strasbourg. The High School Students Union said more than half of France's high schools were blockaded or had closed for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online. Rights groups, students and parent groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and in some places deteriorated into urban violence. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted for unspecified crimes, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said on Monday. "They want to divide the young people into good and bad protesters," said Omar Slaouti, a high-school teacher in Argenteuil, a northwestern suburb of Paris. "If there were no trash cans on fire, the government would not have stepped back and become aware of the issues at stake." PRIME MINISTER PROMISES A RESPONSE Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students' leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks. The government will also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October. Parent Emilie Lhomme said at a protest outside the Helene Boucher school in Paris that the government's words were not enough: "That's all fine and dandy, but that's not what's going to change the daily lives of our children," she said. Finding spare cash to implement educational reforms will be difficult. The government is under pressure to try to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France's growing debt, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push the cost of borrowing higher. The yield on [USN:L8N45O0YO TEXT:"France's 10-year bonds"] briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week. The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the [USN:L6N45S0D2 TEXT:"sliding euro currency"] the latest alarm bell for policy makers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday there was no need for the [USN:S8N3XB0C2 TEXT:"European Central Bank"] to step in. Le Pen, the far-right euro-sceptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring's election, set out [USN:L1N45S0C4 TEXT:"plans to slash public spending if elected"], seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens. French spending on education has lagged inflation and the country's students are trailing their OECD peers in overall performance, data from the[USN:L8N44Z0XI TEXT:" PISA 2025 assessment"] shows.

item.title: Taiwan says it has not heard new US arms sales will be carved into smaller chunks
item.description: Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo said on Tuesday he had not heard that the US was planning on carving up a potential $14 billion arms sale into smaller chunks, but added that Washington's commitments to Taipei's defences had not changed.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo said on Tuesday he had not heard that the US was planning on carving up a potential $14 billion arms sale into smaller chunks, but added that Washington's commitments to Taipei's defences had not changed. US President Donald Trump has held back approval of the new package of arms sales to Taipei in order to maintain warm relations and a fragile trade truce with Chinese President Xi Jinping. In December, Trump approved an [USN:L1N3XN16Z TEXT:"$11 billion package"]. In May, after meeting Xi in Beijing, Trump said he was holding up a [USN:L1N41S025 TEXT:"second package"] and described it as a "very good negotiating chip." China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has repeatedly called for the arms sales to end. Officials in Taipei previously said Washington could [USN:L1N45G08H TEXT:"carve up"] the arms sales into smaller chunks in an effort to avoid upsetting Beijing too much. Speaking in parliament, Koo said the US has repeatedly reaffirmed that its commitment to helping Taiwan strengthen its self-defence capabilities has not changed. "Regarding arms sales, we respect the US review process. We are also continuing to coordinate with the United States. At present, we have not received any information about so-called separate batches," he added, without elaborating. A US State Department spokesperson declined to comment on pending arms sales but added that the administration has been very clear that "the enduring US commitment to Taiwan continues" as demonstrated by its arms sale notification in December. The US is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself and Washington is Taipei's most important international backer, despite an absence of formal diplomatic ties. Koo said Taiwan and the US "do indeed have close exchanges in the military and defence spheres." "This will also help us with our current war-preparedness efforts and the transformation of our armed forces." This week, Taiwanese Foreign Minister [USN:L1N45R00A TEXT:"Lin Chia-lung"] and former President [USN:L4N45O08K TEXT:"Tsai Ing-wen"] are in the US, the latter making her first trip to the country since stepping down two years ago. A US State Department spokesperson said, in response to those visits, that the US and international community as a whole benefit from engagement with Taiwan given its tech prowess and the fact it is a vibrant democracy. The Chinese embassy in Washington reiterated that it "firmly opposes official interactions of any form between China's Taiwan region and the US."

item.title: Wall Street shares notch records as oil prices stabilize, bond yields retreat
item.description: World stocks scaled two-week highs on Tuesday with Wall Street indexes setting new records, as steady oil prices and falling bond yields boosted sentiment and investors looked ahead to an earnings season they expect will be powered by AI-driven growth.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence Delevingne, Medha Singh, Stella Qiu
item.content:encoded: World stocks scaled two-week highs on Tuesday with Wall Street indexes setting new records, as steady oil prices and falling bond yields boosted sentiment and investors looked ahead to an earnings season they expect will be powered by AI-driven growth. The S&P 500 (.SPX) hit a [USN:L6N45S16W TEXT:"fresh record"], up about 0.6% on the day, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq (.IXIC) gained 0.45%, also an all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 0.5%. The pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) [USN:L4N45S182 TEXT:"gained about 0.5%"] and MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) rose 0.6%. Bond markets found [USN:L1N45S0P3 TEXT:"some respite"] on Tuesday after France's contested [USN:L1N45N0A3 TEXT:"budget"] had triggered a French debt rout and fuelled fears of broader stress across the euro zone. The euro rose 0.3% to 1.126, stabilising after hitting a 17-month low in the previous session due to [USN:L6N45S0D2 TEXT:"concerns"] about the euro zone's fiscal outlook. Political uncertainty also deepened after Spain called a [USN:L8N45R05N TEXT:"snap election"] on Monday. France's 10-year bond yield dipped to 4.7% after surging to its highest since the 2000s last week. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in next spring's presidential election, [USN:L1N45S0C4 TEXT:"outlined"] her plans to cut spending if elected in 2027. "On the one hand, you've got quite material pressure being felt on the government bond side. But elsewhere the corporate side of things actually doesn't look too bad. You've got companies whose earnings remain very robust. We're getting into the earnings season fairly soon, expectations for that are pretty high," said James Klempster, deputy head of multi-asset at Liontrust in London. With few major catalysts on this week's calendar, investors are increasingly focused on third-quarter earnings, which begin in earnest next week. Goldman Sachs estimates consensus forecasts imply 27% growth in S&P 500 earnings, with more than half that coming from companies benefiting from AI infrastructure spending. Nvidia (NVDA.O) , the world's most valuable company and a bellwether for the AI trade, ticked up 0.14%, rising closer to a market value of $6 trillion. Brent crude settled slightly higher at about $100.6 a barrel as resilient Middle East [USN:L1N45S05E TEXT:"crude exports"] and a G7 emergency stockpile release eased supply concerns, though ongoing security risks in the region limited losses. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude < CLc1 > rose 1 cent to settle at $89.44. Strategists at PIMCO said in a new outlook that they expect stable global growth to continue while inflation moderates as the energy price shock fades and AI-related demand continues to grow. "The global economy has remained resilient," they wrote. BOND WORRIES LINGER The dollar weakened broadly against most major currencies, reversing some recent advances as investors pared back their bets on US interest rate hikes following a soft US jobs report and policymakers' calls for more [USN:S0N44V01O TEXT:"evidence"] before further tightening. The dollar index fell 0.3%, after rising 3% over the past month. Traders scaled back expectations of a Federal Reserve rate increase this month to 19% from about 50% a week earlier. Long-dated US Treasury yields also [USN:L1N45S0RM TEXT:"eased"] after touching fresh 24-year highs on Monday, amid a persistent selloff since late August on inflation and debt concerns. The 10-year yield fell 2.7 bps to 5.28%, while the 30-year yield dipped 0.5 bps to 5.65%. Spot gold [USN:L1N45S0G9 TEXT:"rose"] 0.7% to $4,168 an ounce.

item.title: Oil prices stable as market weighs supply risks, rising Middle East exports
item.description: Oil prices were little changed on Tuesday after recovering earlier losses, as the market weighed increases in Middle Eastern crude exports and a planned Group of Seven release of emergency diesel and crude stockpiles against supply concerns related to attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
item.dc:creator: Scott Disavino
item.content:encoded: Oil prices were little changed on Tuesday after recovering earlier losses, as the market weighed increases in Middle Eastern crude exports and a planned Group of Seven release of emergency diesel and crude stockpiles against supply concerns related to attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. Brent futures rose 26 cents, or 0.3%, to settle at $100.58 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose one cent to settle at $89.44. Around 12 million barrels per day of crude oil and 2 million bpd of refined products — volumes needed to dampen price pressure — have left the Middle East on tankers in the last seven to 10 days, the [USN:L6N45S0MD TEXT:"CEO of commodity trading giant Vitol"] said on Tuesday. [USN:L1N45S0DH TEXT:"Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman"] said on Tuesday that oil pumped through the East-West Pipeline, which runs to the kingdom's Red Sea export hub of Yanbu, had reached 5.8 million barrels as of Tuesday morning. Oil price declines, however, have been limited by the possibility of further Middle East supply disruptions. [USN:L1N45S0BG TEXT:"Saudi Arabia's airports"] in Jazan and Najran were targeted in two attacks on Monday evening, injuring three people and causing limited damage, the Saudi aviation authority said, as hostilities between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis escalated. The attacks occurred as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pressed a major offensive to retake territory from the Houthis, after weeks of rebel advances, with Riyadh stepping up airstrikes in support of the campaign. Separately, President [USN:L1N45S0UA TEXT:"Volodymyr Zelenskiy"] of Ukraine said on Tuesday that the latest intelligence suggested Russia was preparing a "massive attack." Russia was the world's third-biggest crude oil producer behind the US and Saudi Arabia in 2025, according to US energy data. [USN:L1N45S0RE TEXT:"Sanctions"] designed to keep Russian energy out of global markets have helped support oil prices since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. A deal to end the Russia-Ukraine war could allow Russia to export more energy. In the US, meanwhile, the [USN:AQN2MMYYH TEXT:"National Hurricane Center"] said there was a 100% chance a cyclone could form over the next seven days in the Gulf of Mexico. A storm in the US Gulf could boost oil prices by shutting oil and natural gas production and damaging other energy infrastructure. OIL STOCKS AROUND THE WORLD The [USN:L6N45S0US TEXT:"International Energy Agency"] will meet next week to work out the details of a diesel stock release as market confusion grows over how many barrels Europe and the US plan to make available to address shortages and record-high prices, sources said. The surge in diesel prices has turned the fuel, which underpins trucking, agriculture and industry, into a global political and economic concern. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have curtailed exports and damaged refineries, helping drive the rise in prices. Under pressure from US President Donald Trump , the [USN:L8N45S0QH TEXT:"Group of Seven"] major economies agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves and pledged to refrain from imposing energy export restrictions. With the war in Iran disrupting the flow of Middle East oil supplies, the US Energy Information Administration projected on Tuesday that world petroleum production would drop from a record 106.3 million bpd in 2025 to 101.1 million bpd in 2026, and world oil demand will drop from a record 104.4 million bpd in 2025 to 102.4 million bpd in 2026. In 2027, however, EIA projected world oil supply and demand would rise back to record highs of 109.6 million bpd of production and 104.6 million bpd of consumption. In the US, meanwhile, the oil market was watching for weekly storage reports from the American Petroleum Institute trade group on Tuesday and the EIA on Wednesday. Analysts estimated energy firms added 1.7 million barrels of crude to US storage during the week ended October 2. If correct, it would mark the first time since August that crude stocks increased for three weeks in a row and compare with an increase of 3.7 million barrels in the same week last year and an average increase of 1.7 million barrels over the past five years (2021 to 2025). ,
